Day 1
From Hotel: 20 min → Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos
1. Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos
Chile's foremost contemporary memorial — a striking glass-and-concrete cube designed by Brazilian firm Estudio América, opened in 2010 by President Bachelet. Photographs, testimony, and artifacts document the victims of Pinochet's dictatorship. Victor Jara's last poem spans the entrance wall.

2. Parque Quinta Normal
A 35-hectare urban park founded in 1841 to acclimatize exotic plant species — now a palm-lined refuge home to four museums, a central lagoon with pedal boats, and old-growth trees planted in the 19th century.

36 min · 12 min → Plaza de Armas
3. Plaza de Armas
The founding square laid out in 1541 by Pedro de Valdivia — the original Spanish colonial grid radiates from here. Flanked by the Metropolitan Cathedral, the Central Post Office, and the former Royal Court housing the National Historical Museum. Busy at every hour with chess players and street performers.

Day 2
From Hotel: 16 min → La Moneda
1. La Moneda
Chile's seat of government — a neoclassical masterpiece by Joaquín Toesca completed in 1805, originally the colonial mint. Bombed by the Air Force during the 1973 coup. Visitors walk the exterior courtyards and the underground Plaza de la Ciudadanía which hosts rotating exhibitions.
Read more
Monday - Friday 9:00am - 5:00pm
Closed Saturday & Sunday
~45 min
Free

34 min · 10 min → Cerro San Cristóbal
2. Cerro San Cristóbal
One of the great urban parks of Latin America — Cerro San Cristóbal rises to 880 m with panoramic views across the city to the snow-capped Andes. Ride the 1925 funicular to the summit Virgin Mary statue then glide back down on the cable car over Bellavista rooftops. Parque Metropolitano spans 722 hectares.

Day 3
From Hotel: 15 min → La Chascona
1. La Chascona
The most visited of Pablo Neruda's three Chilean homes, named for the tangled hair of his muse Matilde Urrutia. This Bellavista labyrinth cascades down a hillside packed with Neruda's eccentric collections: ships' figureheads, butterfly specimens, European bar furniture, and the Nobel Prize medal.

23 min · 8 min → Estación Mapocho
2. Estación Mapocho
Built in 1912 by architect Emilio Jecquier — the same architect as the Bellas Artes museum — this iron-and-glass station served passengers until 1987. Today one of Chile's finest cultural venues: its soaring vaulted interior flooded with light through ornate iron trusses is unmissable even without an event on.

3. Sky Costanera
Latin America's tallest building — the 300 m Gran Torre — opens its 61st and 62nd floor observation decks to the public. On a clear day the 360-degree view stretches from the Pacific coast 100 km west to the Aconcagua massif in the Andes with the full sweep of the city below.

Day 4
From Hotel: 16 min → Museo Precolombino
1. Museo Precolombino
One of the finest pre-Columbian collections in the Americas, housed in a restored 19th-century building originally built as the Royal Custom House. Three floors of ceramics, textiles, goldwork, and sculpture from Mesoamerica, the Andes, and the Southern Cone — the Andean and Amazonian galleries are exceptional.

2. Cerro Santa Lucía
A forested urban hill rising from Lastarria, transformed by Intendant Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna in the 1870s from a barren rock into the city's first public park. Terraced gardens, Neo-Gothic fountains, and a hilltop belvedere with sweeping city views.

17 min · 10 min → Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
3. Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
Chile's national fine art museum in a stunning Beaux-Arts building designed for the 1910 centenary. The largest glazed dome in South America floods the central hall with light. Permanent collection spans Chilean painting from the 18th century alongside European works — all free.

39 min · 10 min → Palacio Cousiño
4. Palacio Cousiño
The last intact 19th-century aristocratic palace in Santiago, built in 1878 for the widow of mining magnate Luis Cousiño. French Second Empire design by Paul Lathoud; the interior retains original Baccarat crystal chandeliers, silk wallpapers, and furniture shipped from France. Guided tours in Spanish and English.

Day 5
From Hotel: 13 min → Parque Forestal
1. Parque Forestal
A 16-hectare riverside park planted with century-old plane trees by architect Georges Dubois in 1900. The Fuente Alemana fountain anchors the central promenade; the park connects Lastarria to the chain of parks running east along the Mapocho to Vitacura.
Read more
Open 24/7
~45 min
Av. José Miguel de la Barra · Parque Forestal
15 min → Parque Bicentenario
2. Parque Bicentenario
A 40-hectare riverside park opened in 2007 for Chile's bicentennial, designed by architect Teodoro Fernández around a central lagoon inhabited by black-necked swans. Part of the chain of parks running along the Mapocho from Parque Forestal to Vitacura.
Read more
Daily 8:00am - 8:00pm
~1 hr
Av. Bicentenario 3680 · Vitacura
19 min → Cerro Manquehue
3. Cerro Manquehue
Santiago's highest accessible urban summit at 1,635 m — the ridge separating Vitacura from Lo Barnechea. A round-trip hike from the Vía Roja trailhead climbs through native scrub to panoramic views spanning the full city grid, the Mapocho valley, and the snow-capped Andes. No permits required.
Open 24/7
~2 hr 30 min

Local Tastes
Empanada de pino
Chile's national snack — a half-moon pastry filled with ground beef, onion, olives, hard-boiled egg, and raisins. Best from a neighbourhood bakery or fuente de soda.
Any bakery in Lastarria
Pisco Sour
Chile's national cocktail — pisco, fresh lime, simple syrup, and egg white. Silkier and less citric than the Peruvian version.
Chipe Libre · Liguria
Cazuela
The classic Chilean stew — slow-cooked broth of chicken or beef with potato, corn on the cob, squash, and rice. Served as a complete meal at any traditional picada.
Confitería Torres · El Hoyo
Completo
Chile's hot dog — buried under mashed avocado, sauerkraut, tomato, and mayonnaise. Best from a street stall or fuente de soda.
Fuente Alemana
Mote con huesillos
The unofficial drink of Chilean summer — hulled wheat in a sweet syrup of dried peaches. Sold by street vendors on Cerro San Cristóbal and across the city centre.
Street vendors · Pío Nono · Recoleta

Heads Up
La Chascona — Closed Monday; reserve tickets online
La Chascona is closed Monday. Timed-entry tickets must be reserved in advance to avoid weekend queues.
Cerro San Cristóbal — Funicular queues peak mid-morning
The Parque Metropolitano funicular gets its longest queues between 10:00am and 1:00pm on weekends.
Sky Costanera — Timed-entry sells out; buy in advance
Sky Costanera sells timed-entry tickets online. Friday and Saturday evening slots sell out days in advance.

Worth Knowing

One Coup, Two Losses

Pablo Neruda died of cancer twelve days after the 1973 coup, but the ransacking of La Chascona happened first, while he was still alive. Soldiers broke in, burned his books, and diverted the property's stream so it flooded the house, leaving the floors under mud. When his widow, Matilde Urrutia, insisted on holding his wake there anyway, mourners had to lay wooden planks over the wreckage just to carry his coffin inside. What was meant to intimidate turned into the opposite: his funeral procession, held in plain sight of soldiers patrolling the streets, became one of the first public protests against the new dictatorship.

On the morning of September 11, 1973, President Salvador Allende gave his final address from inside La Moneda while Air Force jets bombed the building around him. He refused calls to resign or evacuate, telling the country over the last working radio signal that he would pay for his loyalty with his life. Within hours the palace had fallen and Allende was dead — by his own hand, according to an autopsy carried out decades later after his remains were exhumed. The palace visitors walk through today was rebuilt afterward and carries almost no visible trace of that morning.
